mainTopic: Which kind of town (announcing non-kosher sales or not) the ברייתא is set in, how the announcement is worded, and why letting someone mislead himself is not deception
overview: This amud finishes a ברייתא about sending meat to a גוי and then asks what kind of town it describes. In some towns, Jewish butchers announce every time they sell non-kosher meat to a גוי. In other towns, they don't. The first and last clauses of the ברייתא seem to fit only a town that does not announce. The middle clause, which worries that a גוי will resell נבלות to a Jew, seems to fit only a town that does announce. אביי accepts that the clauses are set in different kinds of town. רבא puts them all in an announcing town and splits them by whether an announcement was actually made. רב אשי puts them all in a non-announcing town and explains the middle clause as a גזירה, in case a Jew sees the sale. The גמרא then gives the wording of the announcement, 'meat has fallen to the soldiers,' and explains that this is not deceiving the גוים, because they deceive themselves. A story about מר זוטרא, רבא and רב ספרא supports this idea. The amud ends as a new story about a butcher begins, and it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the ברייתא: two reasons for the last rule
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes its last clause, giving two reasons: fear of oppressors, and fear that the seller will hand over נבלות וטרפות.
steps.simpleTranslation: One reason is because of the oppressors, and the other is that perhaps they will sell him נבלות and טרפות.
steps.whatsHappening: We are hearing the last words of a ברייתא that the גמרא quoted. It gives two reasons for its final rule, which deals with a גוי who is sent to buy meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First reason: the אנסין, meaning the גוי may keep the money and force the seller to hand over meat for free. Second reason: the seller may think the גוי is buying for himself and give him נבלות or טרפות, which would then reach the Jew.

keyTerms.meaning: Oppressors, people who take things by force
Animals that died without a kosher שחיטה
Animals with a fatal defect, forbidden even after שחיטה

phrases.english: One, because of the oppressors,
and one, lest they sell him
carcasses and טרפות.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are two reasons for the rule: the oppressors, and the risk of being sold נבלות וטרפות.

steps.title: Quoting the line about a thigh sent to a גוי, and asking what case it describes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ruling that a thigh sent to a גוי does not need its גיד הנשה removed, then asks what situation the ברייתא means.
steps.simpleTranslation: The master said: For a גוי, whether the thigh is whole or cut, one does not need to remove the גיד הנשה. What case are we dealing with?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to one line of the ברייתא and asks what kind of place it is talking about. This sets up the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling seems simple: a גוי may eat the גיד הנשה, so why remove it? But the real worry is that a Jew might later get this meat from the גוי. Whether that can happen depends on local custom, so the גמרא needs to know which town is meant.

keyTerms.meaning: The sciatic nerve in the thigh, which a Jew may not eat
Whole, so the thigh is still recognizable
Cut up, so it is hard to recognize
What case are we dealing with?

phrases.english: The master said: And with a gentile,
phrases.notes: The גמרא is quoting an earlier line of the same ברייתא, about sending a thigh to a גוי.

phrases.english: whether whole or cut,

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ לִיטּוֹל הֵימֶנָּה גִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה.
phrases.english: he does not need to remove the sciatic nerve from it.
With what are we dealing?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the end of the ברייתא back to analyze an earlier clause.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In what kind of place is this ruling set: a place that announces non-kosher sales to a גוי, or one that does not?

steps.title: It can't be a place that announces
steps.stepSummary: If the town announces non-kosher sales, then a cut thigh sold without an announcement could be bought back by a Jew with the גיד still inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it is a place where they announce, why is there no need to remove the גיד הנשה from a cut thigh? Since no announcement was made, a Jew will come to buy it from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the first option, a town where butchers announce, and shows it does not fit the ruling about a cut thigh.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In such a town, Jews rely on the announcement. If none was made, they assume meat a גוי got from a Jewish butcher is kosher. A cut thigh hides the גיד, so a Jew might buy it and eat the גיד הנשה. The ruling not to worry would make no sense there.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (the first option being tested)
They announce, meaning the butchers publicly declare a sale of non-kosher meat to a גוי

steps.confusionAlert: The announcement is about meat that is not kosher. Here the thigh itself is kosher, so nobody announces anything. That silence is exactly why a Jew might trust it and eat the hidden גיד.

phrases.english: If you say in a place where they announce,
phrases.notes: In this kind of town, the Jewish butchers announce whenever they sell non-kosher meat to a גוי.

phrases.english: a cut one, why

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ לִיטּוֹל הֵימֶנָּה גִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה?
phrases.english: does he not need to remove the sciatic nerve from it?
Since they did not announce,
he will come to buy from him.
phrases.notes: "He" is a Jew who buys the meat from the גוי.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the first possible answer to the question.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the ruling about a thigh sent to a גוי is set in a place that announces.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Where announcing is the custom, silence signals kosher meat, so a Jew could buy the cut thigh and eat the גיד.

steps.title: So it must be a place that does not announce
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes the first clause must be set in a town with no announcing custom, where Jews don't buy meat from a גוי at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is obvious that it is a place where they do not announce.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the first option failed, the גמרא switches to the other one: a town that does not announce.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a town with no announcements, Jews cannot tell what a גוי's meat is, so they never buy meat from a גוי. Then sending even a cut thigh to a גוי causes no risk, which fits the ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, which signals a switch to a new answer

phrases.english: Rather, obviously in a place where they do not announce,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by choosing the other kind of place.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (which kind of town)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe the ruling is set in a town that announces.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first clause must be set in a town that does not announce, where Jews never buy meat from a גוי.

steps.title: The middle clause doesn't fit a place that doesn't announce
steps.stepSummary: The middle clause forbids selling נבלות to a גוי in case he resells them to a Jew. In a town with no announcing, no Jew would buy from a גוי, so that worry makes no sense.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say the middle clause: Because of two things they said one may not sell נבלות and טרפות to a גוי: one, because it misleads him, and one, lest he go and sell it to another Jew. And if this is a place that does not announce, no Jew will come to buy from him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the middle clause of the same ברייתא and shows it cannot be set in a town that doesn't announce.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second reason, that the גוי might resell to another Jew, only works if Jews do buy meat from a גוי. That happens only in a town that announces. So the middle clause seems to be set in the opposite kind of town from the first clause.

keyTerms.meaning: Say the middle clause, meaning look at the next part of the source

phrases.english: Say the middle clause:
Because of two things they said
one may not sell carcasses and טרפות to a gentile:
one, because he misleads him,
and one, lest he turn around
and sell it to another Jew.
But if in a place where they do not announce,
surely he will not come to buy from him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 4 by using the next clause of the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא is set in a place that does not announce.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Worrying that the גוי will resell to a Jew only makes sense where Jews buy from a גוי, which happens only in a town that announces.

steps.title: So the middle clause must be a place that announces
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes the middle clause is set in a town that announces, which leaves it clashing with the first clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is obvious that it is a place where they announce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states where the middle clause must be set. This leaves a problem: the first clause and the middle clause now seem to be about different kinds of towns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 placed the first clause in a town that doesn't announce. This step places the middle clause in a town that does. One ברייתא now seems to switch settings between clauses, and the גמרא will need to resolve that next.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious, meaning this is the only option left

steps.whatToRemember: The first clause (cut thigh to a גוי) fits only a town that does not announce. The middle clause (worry about reselling to a Jew) fits only a town that does announce. The ברייתא seems to contradict itself.

phrases.english: Rather, obviously in a place where they announce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the forced conclusion from step 5, which clashes with step 4.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The middle clause is set in a town that announces, while the first clause was set in one that does not. The setting appears to switch within one ברייתא.

steps.title: The last clause cannot be about a town that announces
steps.stepSummary: The סיפא says not to send a גוי to buy meat, because he might be sold נבלות or טרפות. In an announcing town that worry would not exist, because the sale of a טרפה would be announced.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now look at the last clause: A person should not tell a גוי, 'Buy me meat with this coin,' for two reasons. One is because of the oppressors. The other is that he might be sold נבלות or טרפות. But if this were a town that announces, then if the meat were a טרפה, they would have announced it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the last clause of the ברייתא. It shows that this clause cannot fit a town that announces non-kosher sales.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סיפא worries that the גוי might bring home non-kosher meat without the Jew knowing. In a town that announces every non-kosher sale, the Jew would hear the announcement and know. So the worry only makes sense in a town with no announcing.

keyTerms.meaning: The last clause of a teaching
They would surely have announced it

phrases.english: Say the latter clause:
A person should not say to a gentile,
'Buy meat for me with this dinar,'
because of two reasons:
one, because of the oppressors,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֶחָד – שֶׁמָּא מוֹכְרִין לוֹ נְבֵילוֹת וּטְרֵפוֹת,
phrases.english: and the other, in case they sell him unslaughtered carcasses and tereifot,
but if it is in a place where they announce,
if it were the case that it was a tereifa,
they would have announced it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After setting the middle clause in an announcing town (Step 6), the גמרא tests the last clause.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the סיפא could be set in a town that announces
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Announcing would remove the worry about the גוי bringing home טרפה meat, so the סיפא's ruling would have no reason.

steps.title: The three clauses seem split between two kinds of town
steps.stepSummary: So the סיפא must be in a non-announcing town. That puts the first and last clauses in a non-announcing town and the middle clause in an announcing town. Can that be right?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is obvious that this is a town that does not announce. So the first and last clauses are about a town that does not announce, and the middle clause is about a town that announces?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lays out the strange result: the ברייתא keeps switching settings from clause to clause. It sets this up as a problem that needs an answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 4 and 7 put the first and last clauses in a non-announcing town. Step 6 put the middle clause in an announcing town. A single ברייתא jumping back and forth like that seems unlikely, so the גמרא is challenging it.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not the final ruling. It is the problem that אביי, רבא and רב אשי are about to answer.

phrases.english: Rather, it is obvious that it is in a place where they do not announce.
So the first clause and the last clause are in a place where they do not announce,
and the middle clause is in a place where they announce?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from Step 7 and shows the clash it creates.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא as one consistent teaching
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The clauses would have to switch between two kinds of town, which seems unlikely for one ברייתא.

steps.title: אביי accepts the split
steps.stepSummary: אביי says yes: the first and last clauses are about a non-announcing town, and the middle clause is about an announcing town.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Yes. The first and last clauses are about a town that does not announce, and the middle clause is about a town that announces.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers by simply accepting the split. The ברייתא really does switch settings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי does not see the switching as a real problem. A ברייתא can bring together rulings that belong to different kinds of towns.

phrases.english: Abaye said: Yes,
the first clause and the last clause are in a place where they do not announce,
and the middle clause is in a place where they announce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 8 by accepting it.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepting the challenge's result: the clauses are set in different kinds of town.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The switching settings seemed impossible for one ברייתא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The switching is acceptable. The clauses really are set in different kinds of town.

steps.title: רבא sets the whole ברייתא in an announcing town
steps.stepSummary: רבא says all three clauses are about a town that announces. The first and last clauses are about a time when they did announce, and the middle clause is about a time when they did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The whole ברייתא is about a town that announces. The first and last clauses are about when they announced, and the middle clause is about when they did not announce.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different answer that keeps the whole ברייתא in one kind of town. The difference between the clauses comes from whether an announcement was actually made.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבא, the question is not what kind of town it is but whether an announcement was made that day. So one town can fit all three clauses, and the ברייתא no longer switches settings.
steps.whatToRemember: אביי: the clauses are set in different kinds of town. רבא: all the clauses are in a town that announces, and the difference is whether an announcement was actually made.

phrases.english: Rava said:
All of it is in a place where they announce.
The first clause and the last clause are when they announced,
the middle clause is when they did not announce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer from אביי to the same challenge in Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the cases: same town, but different times (announced or not announced).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The clauses seemed to need two different kinds of town.
steps.terutzMaskana: All the clauses fit one announcing town; they differ only in whether an announcement was made.

steps.title: רב אשי: The whole ברייתא is about a town that does not announce
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says all three clauses are about a non-announcing town. The middle clause's ban is a גזירה, in case the sale happens in front of another Jew.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: The whole ברייתא is about a place where they do not announce. The middle clause is a rabbinic decree, in case he sells it in front of a Jew.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a third answer to the clash between the clauses. He puts every clause in a town that does not announce.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי split the clauses between two kinds of towns, and רבא split them by time. רב אשי keeps all three clauses in one setting. He explains that the middle clause bans selling non-kosher meat to a גוי for a different reason: a Jew watching the sale might think this meat is kosher.

keyTerms.meaning: a rabbinic decree made as a safeguard

steps.whatToRemember: There are three answers to the clash. אביי splits the clauses by place, רבא splits them by time, and רב אשי puts them all in one place and calls the middle clause a גזירה.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
The whole ברייתא is about a place where they do not announce,
and the middle clause is a decree
in case he sells it in front of a Jew.
phrases.notes: The worry is that the Jew watching will think this meat is kosher.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: כּוּלַּהּ בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין מַכְרִיזִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer, alongside אביי and רבא, to the clash between the clauses.
steps.terutzResolutionType: One setting for all clauses, with a new reason given for the middle clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The middle clause seemed to need an announcing town, because in a town that doesn't announce no Jew would buy meat from a גוי, so the worry about reselling to a Jew would make no sense (Step 5).
steps.terutzMaskana: All three clauses are in a non-announcing town. The middle clause's ban is a גזירה, in case a Jew sees the sale and thinks the meat is kosher.

steps.title: How exactly is the announcement made?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the wording of the announcement is in towns that do announce.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do we announce?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a side question. It asks what words are used when a town announces that non-kosher meat was sold. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps kept talking about towns that announce. Now the גמרא wants to know what is actually said, which leads into a short back-and-forth.

phrases.english: How do we announce?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the wording of the announcement mentioned in the earlier answers.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact words used to announce a sale of non-kosher meat.

steps.title: The announcement: 'Meat has fallen to the soldiers'
steps.stepSummary: רב יצחק בר יוסף says the announcement is 'meat has fallen to the soldiers.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יצחק בר יוסף said: They announce, 'Meat has fallen to the soldiers.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יצחק בר יוסף answers the question. They announce that some meat is going to the soldiers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Jews in town understand that this meat is not for them. The גוים, who are called the 'soldiers' here, just hear that meat is available. The wording never says out loud that the meat is non-kosher.

phrases.english: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef said:
Meat has fallen to the soldiers.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בַּר יוֹסֵף: נְפַל בִּישְׂרָא לִבְנֵי חֵילָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of how the announcement is worded.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The wording is 'נפל בישרא לבני חילא,' meaning meat has fallen to the soldiers.

steps.title: Why not say plainly that it is a טרפה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the announcement does not simply say 'a טרפה has fallen to the soldiers.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Let them say, 'A טרפה has fallen to the soldiers!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording. Why not just say clearly that the meat is a טרפה?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point of the announcement is to warn Jews. Saying 'טרפה' would seem to warn them more clearly than just saying 'meat.'

phrases.english: But let them say: A טרפה has fallen to the soldiers!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording רב יצחק בר יוסף gave.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Saying 'טרפה' would warn the Jews more clearly, so why not say it?

steps.title: The גוים would not buy it
steps.stepSummary: If they said 'טרפה,' the גוים would not buy the meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: They would not buy it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that if the meat were called 'טרפה,' the גוים would refuse to buy it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller needs the גוים to buy the meat so he does not lose money. The word 'meat' warns the Jews and still lets him sell it.

phrases.english: They would not buy it.
phrases.notes: The גוים would not want an animal the Jews had turned down.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge about the wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Saying 'טרפה' would be the better wording.
steps.terutzMaskana: Saying 'טרפה' would stop the sale, so 'meat' is used instead.

steps.title: Isn't this tricking the גוים?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the vague announcement deceives the גוים.
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn't he deceiving them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new challenge. Hiding that the meat is a טרפה seems to trick the גוים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in the last step was that the wording keeps the גוים from knowing it is a טרפה. That sounds like misleading them on purpose, which the גמרא asks about.

phrases.english: But isn't he deceiving them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer that the wording keeps the גוים buying.
steps.kashyaTarget: Using vague wording so the גוים will buy
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Hiding the meat's status seems to be deceiving the buyers.

steps.title: They deceive themselves
steps.stepSummary: The seller says nothing false. If the גוים assume it is good meat, they have misled themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is they who deceive themselves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the seller does not trick anyone. The גוים draw their own wrong conclusion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The announcement is true, since it really is meat. The seller never claims the meat is kosher, so any mistake comes from the buyers' own assumption.
steps.whatToRemember: The announcement says 'meat has fallen to the soldiers.' It is true, it warns the Jews, and it does not count as deceiving the גוים, because they deceive themselves.

phrases.english: It is they who deceive themselves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the charge of deceiving the גוים.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Places the mistake on the buyer
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The vague wording counts as deceiving the גוים.
steps.terutzMaskana: Nothing false is said, so the buyers' wrong assumption is their own doing.

steps.title: מר זוטרא thinks the רבנן came out to greet him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a story as support. מר זוטרא meets רבא and רב ספרא on the road and assumes they came to honor him.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like the time מר זוטרא, son of רב נחמן, was traveling from סיכרא to בי מחוזא, while רבא and רב ספרא were traveling to סיכרא. They met. He thought they had come out to greet him, so he said: Why did the Rabbis go to so much trouble to come all this way?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a story to back up Step 17, where the seller says nothing false and the buyer misleads himself. Here we see a case where someone reached a wrong conclusion all by himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody told מר זוטרא that the Rabbis came for him. He assumed it from the fact that they met on the road. That is the same setup as the גוים assuming the meat is kosher.

keyTerms.meaning: Toward him, meaning to greet him
To trouble oneself, make an effort

phrases.english: Like this, when Mar Zutra
son of Rav Nachman
was going from Sikhra to Bei Mechoza,
and Rava and Rav Safra
were coming to Sikhra,
they met each other.
He thought
that it was to greet him that they were coming,
he said to them:
Why did the Rabbis need
to go to the trouble of coming all this way?

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּמָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports Step 17's idea that a person can mislead himself
steps.raayaObject: The principle from Step 17: if someone draws a wrong conclusion from words that are true, he has misled himself, and this is not deception
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of מר זוטרא meeting רבא and רב ספרא

steps.title: רב ספרא tells the truth: we did not know you were coming
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא corrects מר זוטרא and says they had not known he was coming.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא said to him: We did not know that the Master was coming. If we had known, we would have gone to even more trouble.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ספרא does not let מר זוטרא keep his mistaken idea. He politely tells him the truth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ספרא adds a kind line: if they had known, they would have made even more effort. Still, the message is that the meeting was not in his honor, and this sets up רבא's complaint.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master, a respectful way to address a scholar

phrases.english: Rav Safra said to him:
We did not know
that the Master was coming;
if we had known,
we would have gone to even more trouble.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב סָפְרָא אֲנַן לָא הֲוָה יָדְעִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רב ספרא answers מר זוטרא's question
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב ספרא openly corrects מר זוטרא's mistaken assumption

steps.title: רבא objects: why did you hurt his feelings?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks רב ספרא why he said this, since it upset מר זוטרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רב ספרא: Why did you say that to him? You made him feel bad.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא challenges רב ספרא's decision to correct מר זוטרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's point is that there was no need to say anything. Telling the truth here only caused hurt feelings.

keyTerms.meaning: You weakened his spirit, you upset him

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
Why did you say this to him,
so that you upset him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב ספרא's correction in Step 19
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ספרא's choice to tell מר זוטרא the truth
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Correcting him caused needless hurt, so it would have been better to stay quiet

steps.title: רב ספרא answers: otherwise we would be misleading him
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא explains that staying silent would have been misleading.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא said to him: But if I had kept quiet, we would have been misleading him!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ספרא defends himself. He felt that letting מר זוטרא keep his wrong idea would count as deceiving him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ספרא holds that silence which lets someone believe something false is a form of deception. This is the same worry the גמרא raised in Step 16 about the vague announcement.

phrases.english: He said to him:
But we would be misleading him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's objection in Step 20
steps.terutzResolutionType: Justification: silence would have been deception
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא thought correcting him was needless and hurtful
steps.terutzMaskana: רב ספרא felt that silence would mean misleading him

steps.title: רבא's reply: he would have misled himself
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that staying silent is not deceiving. מר זוטרא made the assumption on his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא answered: He is the one who would have misled himself.
steps.whatsHappening: This line settles the story and proves the point from Step 17. If someone draws a wrong conclusion on his own, you are not deceiving him by staying quiet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody said they came to greet him, so the mistake would have been entirely his own. This is exactly why the vague announcement about the meat is allowed: the seller says nothing false.
steps.whatToRemember: If you say nothing false and someone reaches a wrong conclusion on his own, that is not deception. He misled himself. This is why the vague meat announcement is allowed.
steps.confusionAlert: This line is רבא answering רב ספרא. It is not רב ספרא continuing to speak, even though the text gives no new speaker label.

phrases.english: He is the one who would be misleading himself.
phrases.notes: This is רבא's reply to רב ספרא, even though the text doesn't say who is speaking.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב ספרא's defense and confirms the principle from Step 17
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A person who draws a false conclusion without being told anything false misleads himself, so others need not correct him

steps.title: A new case begins: a butcher speaks to his friend
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new story about a butcher who said something to another person.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a certain butcher who said to his friend:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move: a new case about a butcher. What he said comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This returns to the main topic of selling meat. This line only introduces who is speaking, and the content of his words follows later.

phrases.english: There was a certain butcher
who said to his friend:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case after the story ends
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Introduces a new butcher story; its content follows
